query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ preheating of the build substrate to an intermediate temperature (approximately 400–600 °C) during laser powder bed fusion of AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce thermal gradients, thus lowering residual stresses and enabling a more uniform microstructure, which in turn leads to improved mechanical properties compared to components fabricated under conventional (room temperature) conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with a metastable as-atomized microstructure and typical composition distribution.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled in-situ substrate preheating (400–600 °C) during the LPBF process.
generation.conditions: Processing of miniature components (<1 cm scale) via LPBF using optimized scanning speeds and low energy densities under an inert atmosphere; comparison tests conducted at identical laser parameters with and without substrate preheating.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced steep thermal gradients lead to minimized residual thermal stresses and allow for controlled microstructural evolution (e.g., reduced microstructural heterogeneity and potentially beneficial local chemical ordering) that can mediate dislocation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the build platform decreases the thermal gradient during layer deposition, thereby reducing rapid cooling rates and associated residual stresses. This moderated thermal environment fosters a more uniform phase distribution and can influence the mobility of dislocations (potentially through reduced lattice distortions and enhanced short-range order effects), ultimately improving the ductility and yield strength of the fabricated component.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional high-thermal-load LPBF processing, components fabricated with substrate preheating are expected to exhibit lower residual stresses, a more homogeneous microstructure, and improved mechanical properties such as higher yield strength and ductility, while also simplifying the thermal management during processing.
generation.baseline: LPBF processing of AlCrFeNiSi powder performed at ambient substrate temperature, which typically results in steep thermal gradients, high residual stresses, and degraded mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected to hold for miniature components processed using LPBF in the specified temperature range (400–600 °C). Effects may vary with changes in part geometry, build size, or for alloys with significantly different thermal properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheat temperature and its effect on in-situ chemical ordering or precipitation kinetics in AlCrFeNiSi are not fully established. The magnitude of the improvements in mechanical properties and stress reduction remains to be quantified across different LPBF parameter sets.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study where two sets of identical miniature components are manufactured via LPBF using AlCrFeNiSi powder. One set is processed using standard ambient substrate temperature (baseline), while the other is processed with the substrate preheated to 400–600 °C. All other processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, and atmosphere) are held constant.
measurements: Quantitative measurement of residual stresses using X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction.
Microstructural analysis (grain size distribution, phase homogeneity) via SEM/EBSD.
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compressive strength, hardness, and ductility tests).
Thermal imaging during processing to confirm reduced thermal gradients.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses (beyond the measurement uncertainty) and fail to exhibit improved mechanical properties or a more uniform microstructure compared to the baseline specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) differentially affect the mobility of screw versus edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) across a wide temperature range, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) and pure Mo and Nb metals. Processing: Machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) with radius cutoff 4.7 Å and max level 14; MC/MD equilibration at 800 K with 10^2 MC swaps every 10^3 MD steps; dislocation mobility simulations via shear stress ramping at 20 MPa per 1.5 ps held constant for 150 ps. Test conditions: Temperatures: 300 K and 2000 K; Stress range: 0 to 1.0 GPa; Shear stress ramp rate: 20 MPa per 1.5 ps; Hold time: 150 ps. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
